papers.title: Posterior Matching Distillation
papers.authors: Hidir Yesiltepe, Julius Berner, Arash Vahdat, Pinar Yanardag
papers.summary: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.

papers.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
papers.authors: Tuna Han Salih Meral, Kaan Oktay, Alec Helbling, Atakan Kara et al.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

papers.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
papers.authors: Weihao Cheng
papers.summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

papers.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
papers.authors: Jinbin Luo, Xiaozhe Yao, Shang Yang, Zhijian Liu et al.
papers.summary: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU–GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20–59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40–3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

papers.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
papers.authors: Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu et al.
papers.summary: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O²LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O²LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O²LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

papers.title: ScaleWorld: High-Resolution World Generation through Shared Prediction and Refinement
papers.authors: Yansong Qu, Wesker Zheng, Quanjian Song, Zhiyuan Zhang et al.
papers.summary: High-resolution generation enables video world models to render fine-grained scene structures and textures, but directly generating high-resolution video incurs substantial computational and memory costs. We present ScaleWorld, a causal video model that unifies low-resolution world prediction and high-resolution refinement within a single shared backbone. By refining its own predictions, ScaleWorld produces high-resolution world videos without requiring a separate refinement model. For each video chunk, the shared backbone first completes a low-resolution prediction and then performs one-step high-resolution refinement conditioned on that prediction. To support efficient streaming generation, we maintain separate causal states with a long low-resolution history for prediction and a short high-resolution history for refinement. To address task interference during distillation, we separate specialist optimization from capability consolidation and introduce task-asymmetric on-policy distillation (TA-OPD). This procedure transfers prediction and refinement behaviors from specialized teachers into a shared student through local velocity matching under their respective sampling and history policies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScaleWorld achieves high-quality world generation with improved computational and memory efficiency.

papers.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
papers.authors: Yiyang Du, Yuxuan Kuang, Qitao Zhao, Yixuan Wang et al.
papers.summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

papers.title: Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation
papers.authors: Deepali Singh, Deepesh Parpani, Aviral Gupta
papers.summary: Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM b1, can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM's frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder's representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation.

papers.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
papers.authors: Amine Lbath, Manan Suri, Aurelien Delaitre, Vadim Okun et al.
papers.summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Complementarity-Based Contact Models for Robotics
papers.authors: Onur Beker, A. René Geist, Michael Posa, Marc Toussaint et al.
papers.summary: Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background. While excellent surveys, monographs, and course notes exist, they mostly address computational mechanics or computer graphics or document a single simulator. To the best of our knowledge, a self-contained pedagogical treatment for robotics, bringing these formulations and their solvers together with complete derivations and a unified notation, does not yet exist. This tutorial addresses this gap by connecting rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact. In particular, we explain how complementarity conditions encode non-penetration and frictional dissipation, determining separation, sticking, and sliding without prescribed contact modes. We distinguish equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations, showing how the latter can introduce artifacts such as lift-off and creep. We examine the existence and uniqueness of motion and contact forces, including the solver's role in selecting among multiple solutions. We then compare first-order and Newton-based methods, explain regularization and proximal strategies, and discuss trade-offs between computational cost, robustness, and physical fidelity. Connections to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation help readers interpret simulation results, choose suitable formulations and solvers, and develop their own contact dynamics routines.

papers.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Kai Lu, Chenyang Ma, Ioannis Havoutis
papers.summary: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

papers.title: Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards
papers.authors: Ana E. Sanchez Villalobos, Michael D. Quinn, Aakash Tyagi, Minh D. Luu et al.
papers.summary: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression's traces against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the tests, yet passing. The framework confirmed 41 as scoreboard escapes with assertions failing on the buggy design and proven on the original.

papers.title: Text-Aware, Vision-Blind: How Multimodal Image Editing Systems Handle Unsafe Inputs
papers.authors: Ziqing Yang, Yixin Wu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
papers.summary: Multimodal image generation systems have made rapid progress and increasingly emphasize content safety. However, their safety mechanisms tend to rely on a single modality and lack joint consideration of both visual content and text prompts, particularly in instruction-guided image editing, where the uploaded image may itself carry risk. We thus introduce EditSafetyBench, a benchmark that measures system-level safety awareness of advanced image editing systems, containing 5,940 image-instruction pairs, covering safe and unsafe images across 11 risk categories and three edit intents. We then probe the benchmark dataset on four systems, including Gemini, GPT, Qwen API, and Qwen Local. Based on our evaluation, we observe a systematic text-vision safety mismatch: Gemini and GPT refuse 87.1% and 81.6% cases containing unsafe-intent editing prompts, while only refusing 24.2% and 22.4% cases with both unsafe images and neutral instructions. At the category level, most risks are considered inconsistently by different systems, e.g., GPT allows 70.4% editing attempts of unsafe political content while Gemini only allows 34.8%. Notably, sexual content shows the strongest visual sensitivity, likely benefiting from mature NSFW identification works. Our findings highlight the need for safety guardrails that jointly reason over both visual and textual modalities in image editing systems.

papers.title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
papers.authors: Hao Vo, Taisei Hanyu, Yuki Ikebe, Pham Tri Quang et al.
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper–object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.

papers.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
papers.authors: Sean Tang, Peiran Wang, Ying Li, Esha Shivakumar et al.
papers.summary: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

papers.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
papers.authors: Mengxiao Wang, Mahbub Alam, Kalyan Nakka, Nitesh Saxena
papers.summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

papers.title: Thinflow: Organizing HPC Benchmarking Campaigns as Rerunnable Directory Trees
papers.authors: Richard Schulze, Ari Rasch, Anna-Lena Roth, Jonas Posner
papers.summary: A benchmarking campaign provides the measurements behind an HPC performance study: code variants are built, swept over core or node counts, and measured repeatedly. Moving such a campaign to another supercomputer or rerunning it months later requires work that is not part of the study itself. Job scripts are adapted to each supercomputer, and what exactly ran is often reconstructed afterwards. We present Thinflow, a small Bash engine for organizing HPC benchmarking campaigns as rerunnable directory trees of tasks and runs. A task is a directory with a short shell script next to the code. For each sweep, one command builds the code, runs the benchmarks, and plots the results. Thinflow derives the execution order from declared dependencies and writes it to a plain-text manifest. Per-supercomputer profiles submit the runs to a workload manager such as Slurm. Each run writes a provenance record of its environment, hardware, and parameters. The engine ships inside the campaign directory, so a campaign stays rerunnable without installing a separate tool and, once completed, may serve as a paper artifact. In a case study, we ran one campaign with identical task files on three Slurm partitions of two supercomputers, on up to 16 nodes. This strong-scaling study of matrix multiplication in C/OpenMP, C/MPI, and Julia/MPI comprises 37 task files with 217 non-comment lines. Its 455 benchmark runs recorded what differed per partition, chiefly profiles and command-line parameters. This suggests that such a campaign needs little structure beyond plain shell files.

papers.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
papers.authors: Yicheng Cai, Taegyu Kim, Peng Liu
papers.summary: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.

papers.title: ACE-Brain-0.7: Learning Execution-Grounded Reasoning for Embodied Agents
papers.authors: Yinhe Wang, Shijun Shi, Feng Pan, Tao Tao et al.
papers.summary: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision–language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question–answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.

papers.title: Visual Attribution Limits and Graded Provenance Auditing in Commercial Video-Generation APIs
papers.authors: Haocheng Mei, Yuchuan Tian, Yingte Shu, Chao Xu et al.
papers.summary: Commercial video-generation APIs bill by model and tier, while intermediaries could substitute cheaper models, lower tiers, or cached clips. What can a delivered file establish about its origin? We combine measurements of passive attribution and cryptographic provenance into a graded audit. We test attribution probes and zero-shot detectors under re-encoding, downscaling, and frame-rate changes, and survey C2PA and GB 45438 metadata across 19 commercial endpoints. Only authenticated provenance supports accusations: tier contradictions or duplicate signed instances under fresh-generation contracts, excluding retries and idempotent returns. Unverifiable signed-endpoint deliveries trigger original-file demands under pass-through clauses; archive-reuse and delivery-parameter screens support review only. Six-model container and bitstream accuracy falls from 83.9% on raw files to 45.3% after uniform re-encoding, using different feature sets. Subsampling real references from 24 to 3 fps raises pooled D3 AUROC from 0.845 to 0.988. Only BytePlus authenticates tier claims under our pinned policy, including 187/187 audited deliveries across three Seedance tiers; tested remuxing and re-encoding leave processed Seedance files unverifiable. The audit identifies authenticated contradictions in 100/100 raw 720p signed tier-swap cases, with zero observed false flags on the tested honest pools.

papers.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
papers.authors: Shibo Zhou, Tianqi Hong, Zheng Yan, He Yang
papers.summary: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

papers.title: Anticipating Future Build Results with BuildPredictor
papers.authors: Christian Macho, Katharina Stengg
papers.summary: Continuous Integration (CI) is a popular programming practice for the seamless integration of code changes into the code base. Using CI, developers benefit from automated assembling and testing of the code after each commit. However, while the frequent integration and building supports developers, it also comes at the high costs of wasting time and resources for minimal changes. In this work, we investigate the potential of reducing the drawbacks by anticipating the build outcome using machine learning techniques. In particular, we propose a random forest model with various features such as changes to the source and build code, and changes to the complexity of the code. We observe that our model shows a good performance in an intra-project and holistic setting yielding a median MCC of 0.82 and 0.86, respectively. We also found that the most important features of our model concern the historical build result information. Additionally, we investigated the development of the performance of our model over time and found that our model can quickly arrive at its peak performance. In an additional experiment, we removed the hard-to-interpret historical build information features and found that our model still yields decent performance while improving the interpretability of it. Summarizing, our model can help to avoid unnecessary build runs by anticipating the build result and thus, save resources.

papers.title: Introducing ReTiNA-Cinema: Real-Time Neuro-Augmented Cinema via Generative AI
papers.authors: Antoine Bellemare-Pepin, Philipp Thölke, Yann Harel, Mar Estarellas et al.
papers.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is currently revolutionizing content creation across various media. Between those who fear it will replace human creativity and those who regard it solely as a tool, many in the creative industries are beginning to view generative AI as a collaborator. Yet interaction with these systems often relies on discrete, turn-based prompting that can interrupt flow and constrain expression to symbolic text. We explore physiological signals as a source of continuous adaptation without explicit commands, as a path toward embodied co-creation. This paper presents ReTiNA-Cinema, a methodological proof-of-concept that integrates electroencephalography (EEG) with generative AI to enable physiologically guided visual modulation of cinematic material. By linking physiological activity to the evolving appearance of a film, the system provides a basis for exploring embodied sense-making, in which viewers' bodily responses contribute to shaping the sensory experience through which they interpret the unfolding scenes. The system combines real-time EEG signal processing with a generative AI pipeline based on Stable Diffusion Turbo for frame-level image transformation. Single-user and two-user configurations map EEG-derived features to prompt selection and transformation strength. ReTiNA-Cinema offers a framework for exploring how the physiology of viewers might influence a film's visual presentation, extending the possibilities for participation in cinematic experiences and storytelling. This system raises questions about the effects on engagement, perceived agency, and emotional response, which remain open to future empirical study. Video illustrations: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMu36WzSQKiVeBnrUdwUAoUhqLqGX3bw and implementation: https://github.com/KairosHive/retina-cinema.

papers.title: StarMPI-SVD: Distributed-Memory Parallel Star-M Tensor SVD
papers.authors: Naman Pesricha, Grey Ballard, Srinivas Eswar, Md Taufique Hussain et al.
papers.summary: The star-M tensor algebra generalizes the optimal compression guarantees of the matrix singular value decomposition (SVD) to higher-order tensors. The t-SVDM-I decomposition is computed using a set of invertible transformations and slice-wise truncated SVDs with a prescribed rank, and its adaptive, multirank variant t-SVDM-II can determine slice-wise ranks to satisfy a prescribed error tolerance. Existing implementations of these algorithms are limited to shared-memory environments, restricting their applicability to modern large-scale datasets. In this work, we present the first distributed-memory implementations of t-SVDM-I and t-SVDM-II, which are generalized to N-way tensors. To address computational and communication bottlenecks, we design asynchronous, non-blocking communication strategies for efficient data redistribution to obtain highly efficient key computational kernels. Strong-scaling experiments demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of our approach (at least 70% parallel efficiency on up to 128 nodes, or 6144 cores), and we apply the star-M compression techniques to a set of application datasets of size up to 768 GB.

papers.title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
papers.authors: Rishabh Ravi, Tony Hong, Chen Wang, Yue Zhu et al.
papers.summary: LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity. To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called Aggron. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate Summarization Queue while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Aggron reduces P99 program latency by 27–31%, and raises throughput by 1.34–1.40×.

papers.title: FFGaussType: Feed-Forward Conversion of Glyph and SVG Geometry into Compact Gaussian Assets
papers.authors: Haoan Feng, Tianfu Wang, Peimeng Guan, Dae Yeol Lee et al.
papers.summary: Immersive 3D content allows text and graphical elements, such as subtitles, annotations, and icons, to be placed inside a scene rather than displayed as flat overlays. Placed this way, they respect occlusion and perspective and take on user-assigned materials and lighting while preserving their original shapes. In Gaussian scenes, however, each new glyph or icon requires its own iterative optimization, which limits scalable content creation. We present FFGaussType, which converts extruded glyph and SVG outlines into Gaussian assets in a single forward pass. A point encoder maps anchors sampled on the known surface to a single feature plane, from which a decoder shared by all assets predicts neural Gaussians carrying surface normals. This separates geometric conversion from material and lighting choices, and the feature plane supports image and video coding for compact delivery. We construct a paired dataset of 27,221 glyph and SVG icon assets with anchors and calibrated normal and silhouette renderings, holding out font families for evaluation. Conversion from prepared anchors takes 9.1 ms per asset, at a fraction of the compute and memory of prior baselines. On unseen font families and test icons, FFGaussType achieves 1.62° normal error and 0.985 silhouette IoU, the best among the compared feed-forward converters, matching the fidelity that per-asset fitting needs thousands of steps to reach. The code and dataset will be released after publication.

papers.title: Rethinking Utility in Differentially Private Visualization: A Channel-Centric Perspective
papers.authors: Jing Yang, Sarayu Pacca, Zhaocong Yang, Liyue Fan
papers.summary: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to protect sensitive data in visualization, but understanding how privacy-induced noise affects visual representations remains fragmented. Prior work has examined the impact of DP noise on specific chart types, yet these findings are typically tied to particular chart types and evaluation settings, making it difficult to generalize across contexts. In parallel, visualization research has long established that visual channels, the visual properties of marks that encode data attributes, differ in perceptual effectiveness under noise-free conditions. However, these principles have not been systematically revisited under DP, where noise is deliberately introduced into the data to protect privacy. In this paper, we present a channel-centric perspective to reframe prior empirical and theoretical results. Our synthesis drawson prior findings to motivate a channel-read-mechanism hypothesis: the utility of DP visualizations may depend on the task-relevant reads made salient by visual channel configurations and DP mechanism choice jointly. Moreover, this perspective highlights the role of channel choice throughout the privacy-preserving visualization pipeline, from disclosure framing and DP algorithm design to utility evaluation and interpretation of noisy outputs. The synthesis also identifies gaps in the existing evaluation literature and highlights research opportunities for channel-aware DP visualization.

papers.title: Static Analysis Guidance for Secure LLM Code Generation
papers.authors: Daniele Lunghi, Alberick Euraste Djiré, Zacharie Chenail-Larcher, Mélissa Tessa et al.
papers.summary: Static analyzers are cheap and widely deployed, which makes their reports a candidate feedback signal for secure LLM code generation. Existing approaches place the analyzer inside an iterative repair loop with intermediate steps, which is costly and makes it hard to isolate the report's effect on the model. We introduce two strategies that give the finding to the model during generation. When the analyzer raises an alert, generation is rolled back, and the finding is inserted either as a code comment (Comment) or in the user message (Steering). We compare them with two iterative approaches and a control without the analyzer, across three models and three Python benchmarks, and we measure security using each benchmark's oracle. Guidance during generation is cheap and can be effective, at 0.9 to 1.9 times the baseline's output tokens against up to 24.1 times for iterative approaches. With DeepSeek-V4.1-flash on RiskyPy, Steering raises the share of functional and secure programs from 52.5% to 64.4%, close to the best iterative approach (66.2%) while using less than a fifth of the tokens. A per-rule analysis shows that rules with a local fix benefit most, and replacing the XML parser is net-positive on two of the three models. The study also identifies when guidance should not be applied. Analyzers flag at most 5.6% of the functional but insecure programs on SecEvalPlus, leaving little guidance to act on. When a static analysis alert (warning or error) contradicts the task, models tend to follow the analyzer and break the program. The two Qwen2.5 models often fail when the fix requires restructuring the code. These results indicate that static-analysis guidance is worth applying with a capable model, on rules with a local fix, and after filtering alerts that conflict with the task specification.

papers.title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation
papers.authors: Zhiyao Xu, Zhanjie Ding, Hongyao Yu, Jingyu Xiao
papers.summary: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.

papers.title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
papers.authors: Yingqi Shi, Junru Lu, Yun Liu, Di Yin et al.
papers.summary: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.

papers.title: Cooling Noisy Population Protocols – Vanishing-Gain Averaging and Localisation under Persistent Errors
papers.authors: Leszek Gąsieniec, Łukasz Kuszner, Paul Spirakis, Grzegorz Stachowiak
papers.summary: We study noise-tolerant coordination in anonymous population protocols whose agents interact in uniformly random pairs, maintain real-valued labels, and have no global clock. Each agent cools its updates using a gain γk=(k+1)-p computed from its own local interaction counter. First, for pairwise averaging with independent communication errors drawn from a fixed centred finite-variance distribution, we prove convergence with probability 1 to a common finite random value for every 1/2<p1, and derive convergence-rate exponents under the same assumptions. Second, for one-dimensional localisation with fixed non-degenerate Gaussian displacement errors, we show that the one-sided RightAlign rule rectifies centred noise and cannot stabilise; a signed update based on the relative-position discrepancy restores convergence to the true agents locations up to one finite random translation. Third, we analyse the setting in which both communication errors and displacement-measurement errors depend on the physical distance between the interacting devices. For additive independent Gaussian errors, the two sources combine into one centred effective error whose variance is the sum of the distance-dependent component variances. The signed updates protocol remains convergent for every fixed finite geometry, and the average combined variance determines the leading common-translation fluctuation. These results distinguish cooling-compatible signed corrections from one-sided updates that turn persistent noise into drift.

papers.title: SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
papers.authors: Anjie Xu, Zixing Wang, Yifeng Cai, Leye Wang
papers.summary: LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabilities through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints. Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time, and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-related. We present SkillBridge, a contract-based workflow with three stages: static analysis, dynamic validation, and repair. SkillBridge first screens 3,270 skill-target-OS cases, covering 1,090 skills across Linux, macOS, and Windows, to find OS-sensitive contract evidence. It then runs dynamic tasks and root-cause review on selected cases to confirm whether a failure is caused by an OS assumption, and repairs the contract field that caused the failure, such as guide text, package scripts, dependencies, or platform declarations. Repair raises the reviewer-judged target-task pass rate from 30.6% to 38.4%, a gain of 7.8 percentage points. A retrospective Linux/macOS budget analysis further shows the efficiency effect: SkillBridge reaches 38 confirmed OS issues with 185 dynamic validations, where uniform random selection would require about 865 validations in expectation.

papers.title: ZoionNET: Low-Power Animal Intrusion Detection Using an Acoustic Deep-Learning Classifier for a Cellular Remote-Sensing System
papers.authors: Prasanna Vijay, Adarsh Gupta, Vansh Panwar, Vatsalya Singh et al.
papers.summary: Crop raiding and village intrusion by elephants and large felids impose a recurring cost on communities along forest boundaries in southern India, and existing camera-based monitoring has proven difficult to sustain on the power budgets available at such sites. We present ZoionNET, a battery-powered sensing node that detects animal intrusion acoustically rather than visually. Audio from an onboard PDM microphone is sampled at 8 kHz, converted to mel-spectrograms on-device, and classified on an Arm Ethos-U55 microNPU by two int8-quantised YOLOv8 models arranged as a two-state machine: a lightweight always-on model runs in a dormant state and gates a four-class species classifier through exponential-moving-average thresholds, so the heavier model runs only when an intrusion is likely. A digital vibration sensor supplies a complementary seismic channel. Inferences leave the node as JSON over a cellular Notecard, reaching a web dashboard and SMS alerts to forest rangers without any local gateway. The two models reach reported accuracies of 0.974 and 0.946 on held-out audio, and a complete node costs USD 133.57 in parts. We report the system as built and deployed, and identify explicitly what has not yet been measured, most notably the energy behaviour that motivates the two-state design.

papers.title: Streaming-AAA: Streaming AAA Game Video Generation at High Resolution, High Frame Rate, and Low Latency
papers.authors: Zhihao Hu, Jianqi Ma, Jun Zhang, Jiayang Bai et al.
papers.summary: Controllable streaming video generation offers a promising route toward interactive game simulation, yet existing methods remain far from practical gameplay. They often fail to jointly achieve high visual fidelity, high frame rates, and low interaction latency, resulting in poor responsiveness and degraded user experience. We present Streaming-AAA, a new paradigm for controllable infinite generation of AAA-quality game videos. Our system generates 1080p gameplay videos at 43 FPS with 198 ms end-to-end latency interaction on merely NVIDIA A800 GPUs, while supporting long-horizon play without severe temporal degradation or collapse. Streaming-AAA is built upon three key designs. First, we redesign the VAE architecture for efficient high-resolution decoding, enabling real-time synthesis at 1080p. Second, we pretrain the diffusion model using diffusion forcing and significantly extend the temporal training horizon, allowing the model to capture long-term dependencies and maintain persistent memory. Third, we perform post-training distillation and memory compression to improve inference efficiency while retaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Experiments show that Streaming-AAA substantially improves visual fidelity, frame rate, latency, and long-term stability over prior controllable video generation approaches, enabling a significantly more playable experience for interactive AAA game video generation.

papers.title: Presenting Your Figures: Data-informed Animated Transitions Across Scientific Figure Panels
papers.authors: Lu Ying, Can Liu, Yuxiao Yang, Jianing Yin et al.
papers.summary: Multi-panel figures are commonly used in research papers to show scientific data, and researchers often reuse them when presenting their work. Presenting these figures often involves explaining how data across chart panels are related. Animated transitions can progressively reveal these relationships, but two static panels specify only the endpoints, leaving what intermediate keyframes should show and how the transition should progress unclear. To support transition design across diverse scientific figures, we developed Figure Space and Transition Space through iterative analysis of 48 published multi-panel figures across eight scientific subject areas. Figure Space represents panel composition, data transformations, and visual encodings while retaining the links needed to trace panel results back to records. Transition Space uses this representation and source data to construct and sequence keyframes that make corresponding data visible and align them while preserving the meaning of each panel's position encodings. Building on these spaces, we developed FigFlux, a human-in-the-loop authoring system that guides AI agents in generating animated transitions from a multi-panel figure and its associated materials. Researchers can revise keyframes in natural language before animation generation. We evaluate FigFlux through cross-domain case studies, a study with 16 scientific authors, and expert assessment. Authors reported lower overall workload than with their familiar tools, while experts gave FigFlux transitions higher ratings than transitions created with participants' familiar tools or generated by AI alone. The example gallery have been published online: https://figflux.github.io.

papers.title: Blind tests of a simple-body model of submarine target strength on open benchmarks
papers.authors: Sunil Tyagi
papers.summary: Finite-element and boundary-element models of a submarine's sonar echo need a mesh and a solver, and their cost grows quickly with frequency. SSR-Sim takes an analytical route. The hull is cut into a few simple bodies, the echo of each is a closed-form result of geometrical acoustics or of the Kirchhoff approximation, the surface enters through a plane-wave reflection coefficient, and the echoes add in energy. This paper describes the method, including the reduction of a hull and its sail to simple bodies, and tests it on three open cases. (1) The reflection coefficient of a 50 mm rubber tile on steel plating, computed with finite elements by Yang et al., is reproduced to 0.02 rms or better at incidence angles from 0° to 75° once the layer is allowed to refract. (2) For the rigid full-scale BeTSSi submarine at 1 kHz, a prediction fixed before the reference was opened agrees with the boundary-element results of Venås and Kvamsdal to within 0.7 dB in every aspect sector from the bow to 150°; in the stern sector it is 5 dB high. (3) For a 1:15 BeTSSi model with 10 mm tiles measured in a lake, a second blind prediction is within -3.1, +1.4 and -0.5 dB of the measured level over aspects 0-120° at 5, 15 and 20 kHz, against -3.1, +3.1 and +3.5 dB for the Kirchhoff-finite-element computation published with the measurement. At 10 kHz, on a resonance of the tile, the prediction is 6.9 dB low, and in the bow sector it is 7 dB or more low at every frequency. The tests cover the specular component and the coating model only. The failures show what such a model lacks: edge diffraction and the returns that set the off-beam floor of a real model.

papers.title: Barriers to GenAI Integration During Large-Scale Agile Transformation: An Exploratory Case Study
papers.authors: Nils Brede Moe, Marthe Berntzen, Astri Barbala, Viktoria Stray
papers.summary: Organizations undergoing large-scale agile transformations are increasingly introducing generative AI (GenAI) tools into everyday work. While GenAI promises to accelerate software development, less is known about how organizations integrate GenAI into existing large-scale agile ways of working and how it interacts with tensions related to autonomy, alignment, learning, and coordination. We examine barriers to GenAI integration through an exploratory case study of a large Nordic media organization undergoing a large-scale agile transformation. The findings reveal team-level barriers, including diverging AI beliefs, lack of shared practices, and limited experimentation capacity, and organizational-level barriers, including uneven AI maturity, weak organizational learning mechanisms, and cross-unit coordination and alignment challenges. Our findings suggest that GenAI does not create new organizational challenges but becomes intertwined with existing tensions in large-scale agile transformation and may intensify challenges related to learning, coordination, governance, and trust. We contribute to large-scale agile transformation research by showing how GenAI interacts with ongoing organizational change and by identifying conditions for sustainable GenAI integration at scale.

papers.title: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say
papers.authors: Jongbhin Woo, Jaewook Jeong, Joon Son Chung
papers.summary: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.

papers.title: AGSR: Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution for Gaussian Splatting
papers.authors: Ayman Alkhateeb, Hadi Amirpour, Christian Timmerer
papers.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis, but Gaussian rasterization attenuates fine-scale scene structure through the projected covariance of each primitive. We show that contracting these projected covariances at inference time can mitigate the effective bandwidth limitation induced by finite Gaussian footprints, motivating a multi-aperture rendering framework for super-resolution. Based on this insight, we propose AGSR (Aperture-Guided Super-Resolution), a lightweight inference-time framework that progressively fuses multi-aperture renderings using uncertainty-guided feature aggregation and geometric conditioning from transmittance and depth cues. AGSR operates as a plug-in enhancement for pre-trained 3DGS models. Experiments on the Mip-NeRF 360 benchmark show that AGSR outperforms lightweight image-space super-resolution baselines, with gains increasing as the underlying Gaussian representation deteriorates. The results provide evidence that covariance contraction exposes bandwidth-sensitive structural cues attenuated by native Gaussian rasterization. AGSR achieves these improvements while maintaining real-time performance with up to 139k parameters.

papers.title: Ground Truth Bias in AI-Assisted Medical Annotation: A Crossover Study Using an Independent Radiologist Reference Standard
papers.authors: Márton Baltay, Tamás Ilcsik, Márton Borbély
papers.summary: Behavioural evaluations of artificial-intelligence-assisted annotation score every human decision against a reference standard, so their conclusions inherit that standard's validity. We tested how far conclusions about assistance, reliance and individual differences depend on it. Fifty-one non-expert high-school students annotated 50 knee radiographs for osteoarthritis, with and without a deliberately imperfect classifier, in a crossover design; personality and non-verbal reasoning were also measured. Decisions were scored against the public repository labels and against an independent reference standard from a radiologist panel, which graded 23 of the 50 images as indeterminate. Against the repository labels, assistance raised accuracy from 60.4% to 65.3% (odds ratio 1.23, p=0.002). Against the independent standard, the gain on the 27 determinate images was smaller and not significant in the primary model (78.4% to 80.8%; odds ratio 1.16, p=0.178). The apparent benefit had been concentrated on the indeterminate images and was not significant when those images were assigned to either class. The direction of residual over-reliance depended on how indeterminate cases were handled, and the personality trait most strongly associated with accuracy changed identity and sign between standards. Reliance measures are only as valid as the reference standard that defines when the assistant is right.

papers.title: ContextRenderer: Dynamic-Context Video Generation for Interactive Game Worlds
papers.authors: Runze Wang, Fei Zha, Bing He, Ke Xu et al.
papers.summary: Interactive game world models separate executable world evolution from visual generation, using video models to render engine-provided scene representations into detailed observations. During sustained gameplay, however, existing generative renderers struggle to follow changing conditions while preserving visual continuity across diverse proxies and target styles. We therefore introduce ContextRenderer, an autoregressive video diffusion framework designed for both dynamic conditioning and cross-proxy generalization. It couples Dynamic-Context Learning (DCL) for chunk-level interaction supervision with Recurrent History Compression (RHC) to follow condition updates while preserving visual continuity within a bounded token budget. Across proxy representations, Cross-Representation Flow Alignment (CRFA) connects proxy reconstruction with appearance and interaction variation through a shared high-fidelity reconstruction. WorldPrism, our interaction-centric dataset constructed from agent-built worlds, AAA gameplay, and open-source videos, supplies the corresponding renderings and chunk-level annotations for these learning tasks. Experiments on GWM-Bench and Solar-Bench show improved reconstruction and visual quality, while qualitative results demonstrate minute-long interactive rendering under changing prompts and subject references. Project page: https://rainzor.github.io/contextrenderer/

papers.title: PSM-WSM: Predictively Sufficient Multimodal World Social Modeling
papers.authors: Chunlei Meng, Zhenyu Yu, Pengbin Feng, Jacqueline J. Pang et al.
papers.summary: Learning latent states that support future evolution remains an open problem for multimodal interactive systems. Existing approaches typically optimize representations for current semantic understanding or direct prediction, without explicitly defining what information a latent state should preserve to remain predictive of future dynamics. In this work, we investigate this problem through the principle of predictive sufficiency, which defines a predictive state as a latent variable that retains future-relevant information from historical multimodal observations while reducing redundant dependence on the observed history. Based on this principle, we propose Predictively Sufficient Multimodal Social World Modeling (PSM-WM), a framework that jointly learns predictive latent states and their stochastic temporal evolution through probabilistic state inference, event-conditioned transitions, and multi-step consistency optimization. Beyond forecasting performance, we introduce state-centric evaluations to measure whether learned representations satisfy predictive state properties, including predictive closure, residual history gain, and future semantic alignment. Experiments on Hi-EF, IEMOCAP, MELD, and Ego4D show that PSM-WM improves future multimodal interaction modeling and learns latent states with stronger predictive properties and robustness. These results indicate that predictive sufficiency provides an effective principle for constructing future-oriented multimodal states and highlight the importance of state construction in multimodal world modeling.

papers.title: From Attention to Semantics: Detecting and Mitigating Sound Event Hallucinations in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.authors: Tianyi Sun, Minghao Lv, Chunyang Yu, Shenyue Wang et al.
papers.summary: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) excel at diverse audio tasks, yet remain prone to hallucinating sound events absent from the input. Prior work links such hallucinations to insufficient audio attention. However, we find that real and hallucinated events can receive comparable audio attention mass while attending to different audio positions. To examine whether the attended representations support the generated events, we adapt LatentLens to retrieve neighboring contextualized text representations. The retrieved contexts reveal semantic support for real events, but a semantic mismatch between hallucinated events and their attended audio representations. Directly masking the corresponding audio regions can suppress hallucinated events at the cost of real content. We are motivated by these findings to introduce an explainable and training-free detect-then-mitigate framework for effectively hallucination detection and mitigation that aggregates semantic support and applies differential audio masking to protect regions associated with events predicted to be supported. Extensive experiments on three LALMs and two datasets demonstrate that our method significantly improves hallucination detection and hallucination mitigation performance.

papers.title: Sonic Palette: Predicting Dynamic Color Themes from Music
papers.authors: Wen-Li Wei, Kenneth Yang, Jen-Chun Lin
papers.summary: We present Sonic Palette, a music-driven framework for predicting time-varying color themes from audio. Rather than treating music-to-palette generation as a static problem, our method formulates music–color correspondence as a cross-modal sequence prediction task that models how palette-level visual attributes evolve over time in response to music. Specifically, Sonic Palette uses a music-conditioned autoregressive Transformer to predict frame-wise color themes, each represented by five dominant colors, from input audio features. To support this task, we curate a dataset of paired audio–color sequences derived from 265 full-length official music videos. We further visualize the predicted color themes through a palette-guided recoloring process that preserves image structure while revealing temporally varying color appearance associated with the music. Quantitative results show that Sonic Palette predicts color themes that more closely match the ground truth, while subjective results indicate more natural temporal color transitions and stronger perceived music–color atmosphere alignment, highlighting its potential for music-driven visual design, computational art, and creative visual authoring.

papers.title: Embodied Human-Data Interaction
papers.authors: Niklas Elmqvist
papers.summary: We propose the concept of human-data interaction (HDI) as the human manipulation, analysis, and sensemaking of large, unstructured, and complex datasets. We then proceed to suggest an embodied approach to HDI to build physical reasoning environments for these difficult and polymorphic tasks. We illustrate our approach with two examples: tangible lenses for visual exploration, and an educational computer game with tangible bricks.

papers.title: From Reliance to Overreliance: Taxonomizing and Detecting Relational Risks in AI Companionship
papers.authors: Viet Cuong Nguyen, Fiona Li, Chang Wan, Sheyril Agarwal et al.
papers.summary: Companion AIs are increasingly used for emotional support, yet distinguishing meaningful engagement from harmful reliance remains difficult. We introduce the Taxonomy of Relational Risks (TRR), which operationalizes users' emotional overreliance (EO) as observable conversational behaviors and separately identifies evidence of relational harm (RH), enabling empirical examination of when reliance behaviors co-occur with adverse consequences. Using naturalistic Character.AI and Replika conversations from 110 adults, we found EO-related behaviors in 63.2% of non-roleplay conversations, while observable relational harms appeared in 10.5%. Although EO did not necessarily lead to harm, recurring patterns often co-occurred with harmful outcomes, suggesting value as risk indicators. Open-source LLMs satisfactorily detected 12 of 14 EO behaviors in at least one configuration. Qualitative analysis revealed expectations of care, repeated support seeking, dependency, distress, and reduced confidence in personal judgment. We argue for graduated safety interventions tailored to patterns and trajectories of EO-related behavior.

papers.title: SceneAnything: Agentic Reconstruction of Large-Scale Mesh Scenes from a Single Video
papers.authors: Bowen Xue, Saeed Hadadan, Fabrice Rousselle, Zahra Montazeri et al.
papers.summary: Reconstructing an editable 3D scene from video requires matching visible structure while plausibly completing unseen surfaces. Agents can write scene-construction programs, but direct reconstruction attempts often produce errors in layout, scale, and lighting. We introduce SceneAnything, an automated system for reconstructing mesh scenes from real and generated videos, enabling text-to-scene construction when paired with video generation. A software harness coordinates agents, pretrained vision models, and graphics tools through an explicit reconstruction protocol. Shared camera, depth, and segmentation estimates ground component construction: a scene-owner agent plans the environment and briefs authors, who write parameterized Blender programs. A visibility- and fit-based level-of-detail rule selects the construction level, while unseen regions are completed and marked as inferred. Assembled scenes use fitted lighting and supported motion, and revisions undergo programmatic checks and independent visual comparisons. Accepted programs and lessons are reused across scenes. We evaluate on 100 scenes; subset comparisons show improved original-view fidelity over direct-agent reconstruction and higher novel-view content similarity than the compared video-to-3D methods. We will release the harness, agent instructions, reusable libraries, and scenes.

papers.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
papers.authors: Jia Chen, Yecheng Lv, Xinrong Hu, Jun Bai
papers.summary: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.

papers.title: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers
papers.authors: Arman Bolatov, Nikolay Spitsyn, Daniil Medyakov, Vladimir Aletov et al.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates predict the aerodynamic forces on a car in seconds, compared with hours for a CFD simulation, but training them requires thousands of CFD simulations of different car designs, which car manufacturers keep proprietary. Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. Code: https://github.com/armanbolatov/fedmarsdrivaernet

papers.title: ScaleDiag: Diagnosing the Limits of Test-Time Scaling in GUI Grounding
papers.authors: Chen Liu, Zhen Fang, Xin Yu, Dadong Wang et al.
papers.summary: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1–11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement.
